```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/helpers.R")
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(BayesFactor)
  library(patchwork)
})
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = "center")
```

::: {.callout-important title="Predict first"}
Six labs ran Study 1. Two found *p* < .05, three did not, and one estimate went the wrong direction. Did the effect replicate?
:::

```{r}
#| label: s4-labs
labs <- read.csv("data/story_labs.csv")
lab_stats <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(labs, labs$lab), function(d) {
  s <- two_group(d)
  data.frame(lab = d$lab[1], n = s$n1, diff = s$diff, se = s$se, lo = s$ci[1], hi = s$ci[2], p = s$p,
             bf10 = extractBF(bf_default(d))$bf)
}))
knitr::kable(transform(lab_stats, diff = round(diff, 2), se = round(se, 3), lo = round(lo, 2), hi = round(hi, 2),
                       p = fmt_p(p), bf10 = fmt_bf(bf10)),
             col.names = c("Lab", "n / group", "Diff", "SE", "95% CI lo", "95% CI hi", "p", "BF10"))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Explainer: vote counting, fixed-effect meta-analysis, sequential updating"}
- **Vote counting:** tallying how many studies were significant. It ignores effect sizes and precision, and with modest power it will often report "mixed results" for a real effect.
- **Fixed-effect meta-analysis:** a weighted average of the study estimates, with weights of 1 / SE², so more precise studies count more. It assumes every lab estimates the same true effect. When labs' true effects differ, a **random-effects** model estimates that variation too.
- **Sequential updating:** with normal approximations, each lab's posterior (a mean and an SD) becomes the prior for the next lab.
:::

Counting significant results ("vote counting") says 2 of 6. Combining the evidence says something else. Two ways to combine:

- **Fixed-effect meta-analysis (frequentist):** weight each lab by 1 / SE² and average.
- **Sequential Bayesian updating:** start from a prior, update with lab 1, and let *yesterday's posterior be today's prior* (Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2018) for lab 2, and so on.

```{r}
#| label: s4-accumulate
cumulate <- function(prior_mean, prior_sd) {
  m <- prior_mean; s <- prior_sd; out <- NULL
  for (k in seq_len(nrow(lab_stats))) {
    u <- update_normal(m, s, lab_stats$diff[k], lab_stats$se[k]); m <- u[["mean"]]; s <- u[["sd"]]
    out <- rbind(out, data.frame(after_lab = k, mean = m, lo = m - 1.96 * s, hi = m + 1.96 * s,
                                 p_pos = pnorm(0, m, s, lower.tail = FALSE)))
  }
  out
}
fe <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(lab_stats)), function(k) {
  w <- 1 / lab_stats$se[1:k]^2; m <- sum(w * lab_stats$diff[1:k]) / sum(w); se <- sqrt(1 / sum(w))
  data.frame(after_lab = k, mean = m, lo = m - 1.96 * se, hi = m + 1.96 * se, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(m / se)))
}))
vague <- cumulate(0, 10)
skept <- cumulate(0, 0.25)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Method = c("Fixed-effect meta-analysis", "Bayes, vague prior N(0, 10)", "Bayes, skeptical prior N(0, 0.25)"),
  Estimate = sprintf("%.3f", c(fe$mean[6], vague$mean[6], skept$mean[6])),
  `95% interval` = sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", c(fe$lo[6], vague$lo[6], skept$lo[6]), c(fe$hi[6], vague$hi[6], skept$hi[6])),
  `p or P(effect > 0)` = c(ifelse(fe$p[6] < .001, "p < .001", sprintf("p = %s", fmt_p(fe$p[6]))), sprintf("%.4f", vague$p_pos[6]), sprintf("%.4f", skept$p_pos[6])),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "lccc")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-labs
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Left: each lab's estimate and 95% CI; filled points are p < .05, open points are not. The diamond is the fixed-effect pooled estimate. Right: the combined estimate after each lab, from a fixed-effect meta-analysis and from sequential Bayesian updating with a vague or skeptical prior."
fp <- lab_stats; fp$lab_f <- factor(paste("Lab", fp$lab), levels = rev(c(paste("Lab", 1:6), "Pooled")))
fp$sig <- ifelse(fp$p < .05, "p < .05", "p ≥ .05")
pool <- data.frame(lab_f = factor("Pooled", levels = levels(fp$lab_f)), est = fe$mean[6], lo = fe$lo[6], hi = fe$hi[6])
pF <- ggplot(fp, aes(y = lab_f)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = pal[["gray"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0, linewidth = 0.9, color = pal[["ink2"]]) +
  geom_point(aes(x = diff, shape = sig), size = 3.6, color = pal[["blue"]], fill = pal[["blue"]], stroke = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(x = hi, label = sprintf("p = %s", fmt_p(p))), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.8, color = pal[["ink2"]]) +
  geom_errorbarh(data = pool, aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0, linewidth = 1.2, color = pal[["ink"]]) +
  geom_point(data = pool, aes(x = est), shape = 23, size = 5, fill = pal[["ink"]], color = pal[["ink"]]) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("p < .05" = 21, "p ≥ .05" = 1)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.8, 1.6)) +
  labs(x = "Difference (scale points)", y = NULL, title = "Six labs, one pooled estimate") +
  theme_demo()
acc <- rbind(transform(fe[, 1:4], how = "Fixed-effect meta-analysis", off = -0.18),
             transform(vague[, 1:4], how = "Bayes, vague prior", off = 0),
             transform(skept[, 1:4], how = "Bayes, skeptical prior", off = 0.18))
acc$how <- factor(acc$how, levels = c("Fixed-effect meta-analysis", "Bayes, vague prior", "Bayes, skeptical prior"))
accl <- data.frame(how = levels(acc$how), x = 0.45, y = c(1.5, 1.36, 1.22))
accl$how <- factor(accl$how, levels = levels(acc$how))
pC <- ggplot(acc, aes(after_lab + off, mean, color = how)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = pal[["gray"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.36, color = pal[["gray"]], linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.45, y = 1.08, label = "- - -  truth (0.36)", hjust = 0, color = pal[["ink2"]], size = 4) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8) +
  geom_text(data = accl, aes(x = x, y = y, label = how), hjust = 0, size = 4, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Fixed-effect meta-analysis" = pal[["ink2"]], "Bayes, vague prior" = pal[["blue"]],
                                "Bayes, skeptical prior" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:6) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.3, 1.6), xlim = c(0.4, 6.4)) +
  labs(x = "Labs combined so far", y = "Combined estimate (points)", title = "Evidence accumulates") +
  theme_demo()
pF + pC + plot_layout(widths = c(1.1, 1))
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="How to read this figure"}
1. **Left (a forest plot):** each row is one lab's estimated difference with its 95% CI. Filled dots reached *p* < .05; open dots did not. The black diamond is the pooled estimate from all six labs.
2. Most of the open-dot intervals include the pooled estimate: a nonsignificant lab is not evidence against the effect.
3. **Right:** the combined estimate as labs are added one at a time (1 = lab 1 alone; 6 = all six). Each color is one way of combining; the bars are 95% intervals. The dashed line is the true effect built into the simulation.
4. The gray (meta-analysis) and blue (vague-prior Bayes) results are the same numbers. The orange (skeptical-prior) results start lower and move toward them as data accumulate.
:::

```{r}
#| label: s4-pooled-bf
# One Bayes factor for all 610 participants (305 per group); reasonable here because the labs share one true effect
bf_default(labs)
```

With a vague prior, sequential Bayesian updating reproduces the fixed-effect meta-analysis to the third decimal. The skeptical prior starts lower and moves toward the others as labs accumulate: the prior's weight shrinks as data grow (Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2018, Example 4).

::: {.callout-tip title="What each framework lets you say"}
- **Frequentist:** "Pooling six labs, enjoyment was `r sprintf("%.2f", fe$mean[6])` points higher after the rewarded ending, 95% CI [`r sprintf("%.2f", fe$lo[6])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", fe$hi[6])`]."
- **Bayesian:** "After six labs, even a skeptic's posterior probability that the effect is positive exceeds `r if (skept$p_pos[6] > .999) "99.9" else sprintf("%.1f", 100 * skept$p_pos[6])`%."
- **Neither:** "Only two of six labs replicated the effect." That sentence confuses the significance of each study with the evidence of all of them.
:::

**Theory-building takeaway.** Theories are built across studies, not within one. Bayesian updating makes accumulation explicit, and meta-analysis does the same job with long-run guarantees. If labs differ in their true effects (the "for whom and where" question), the natural next step is a **hierarchical model** that estimates the variation itself.

::: {.callout-warning title="Your turn"}
1. Drop lab 6 (the "failed" replication). How much does the pooled estimate move? What would a literature that only published labs 2 and 5 conclude?
2. Use lab 1's posterior as the prior for Study 1's n = 150 data. Is that legitimate here? What would make it illegitimate?
:::
